claim: MET receptor was discovered three decades ago.
source: The Hepatocyte Growth Factor-Scatter Factor (HGF/SF) receptor MET was discovered three decades ago.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction providing historical context.

claim: MET is important during embryogenesis and injury repair.
source: Its importance was highlighted during embryogenesis and injury repair, and also in neurodegenerative diseases and cancers (Furlan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Furlan et al., 2014.

claim: MET is important in neurodegenerative diseases and cancers.
source: Its importance was highlighted during embryogenesis and injury repair, and also in neurodegenerative diseases and cancers (Furlan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Furlan et al., 2014.

claim: MET activation triggers survival, proliferation, and migration.
source: MET activation triggers a wide variety of biological responses such as survival, proliferation, and migration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about MET's biological functions.

claim: The HGF/SF-MET pair plays a crucial role in the liver during development.
source: The HGF/SF-MET pair notably plays a crucial role in the liver, both during development (Maina et al., 2001) and, in adults, in tissue homeostasis and regeneration (Borowiak et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maina et al., 2001.

claim: The HGF/SF-MET pair plays a crucial role in the liver in adults for tissue homeostasis and regeneration.
source: The HGF/SF-MET pair notably plays a crucial role in the liver, both during development (Maina et al., 2001) and, in adults, in tissue homeostasis and regeneration (Borowiak et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Borowiak et al., 2004.

claim: MET receptor can promote apoptosis in addition to its survival role.
source: In addition to the survival role of ligand-activated MET, the receptor can also promote apoptosis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about MET's dual function.

claim: MET is classified as a dependence receptor.
source: This has led to classifying it as a dependence receptor.
evidence: This is a direct statement about MET's classification.

claim: MET cleavage by caspases leads to production of p40MET, a 40 kDa intracellular fragment.
source: MET cleavage by caspases leads to production of p40MET, an intracellular 40 kDa fragment that can amplify apoptosis, detected in apoptotic primary hepatocytes and mouse livers (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: p40MET can amplify apoptosis.
source: MET cleavage by caspases leads to production of p40MET, an intracellular 40 kDa fragment that can amplify apoptosis, detected in apoptotic primary hepatocytes and mouse livers (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: p40MET is detected in apoptotic primary hepatocytes and mouse livers.
source: MET cleavage by caspases leads to production of p40MET, an intracellular 40 kDa fragment that can amplify apoptosis, detected in apoptotic primary hepatocytes and mouse livers (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: Caspase cleavage of MET occurs at the C-terminal DNID1374 site in mouse sequence.
source: Caspase cleavage of MET occurs at the C-terminal DNID1374 and the juxtamembrane ESVD1000 sites (mouse sequence).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specific cleavage sites.

claim: Caspase cleavage of MET occurs at the juxtamembrane ESVD1000 site in mouse sequence.
source: Caspase cleavage of MET occurs at the C-terminal DNID1374 and the juxtamembrane ESVD1000 sites (mouse sequence).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specific cleavage sites.

claim: The juxtamembrane caspase cleavage site overlaps with the DY1001R site containing a phosphorylated tyrosine responsible for CBL recruitment.
source: The juxtamembrane site overlaps with the DY1001R site containing a phosphorylated tyrosine (ESVD1000p-Y1001R) responsible for the recruitment of CBL involved in the receptor degradation (Peschard et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peschard et al., 2004.

claim: CBL is involved in MET receptor degradation.
source: The juxtamembrane site overlaps with the DY1001R site containing a phosphorylated tyrosine (ESVD1000p-Y1001R) responsible for the recruitment of CBL involved in the receptor degradation (Peschard et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peschard et al., 2004.

claim: C-terminal caspase cleavage of MET removes only five amino acids in mice.
source: Although C-terminal caspase cleavage of MET removes only five amino acids in mice, a p40MET fragment to which these C-terminal amino acids remain attached loses its apoptotic potential (Foveau et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cleavage product.

claim: A p40MET fragment with C-terminal amino acids still attached loses its apoptotic potential.
source: Although C-terminal caspase cleavage of MET removes only five amino acids in mice, a p40MET fragment to which these C-terminal amino acids remain attached loses its apoptotic potential (Foveau et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Foveau et al., 2007 and Ma et al., 2014.

claim: p40MET amplifies apoptosis through mitochondrial membrane permeabilization leading to release of pro-apoptotic factors.
source: The p40MET fragment amplifies apoptosis through mitochondrial membrane permeabilization leading to the release of pro-apoptotic factors.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanism of p40MET action.

claim: Mitochondrial permeabilization is regulated by anti-apoptotic BCL2-family proteins.
source: Mitochondrial permeabilization is regulated by anti-apoptotic BCL2-family proteins and by pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins such as BAX and BAK (Wei et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2001.

claim: Mitochondrial permeabilization is regulated by pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins such as BAX and BAK.
source: Mitochondrial permeabilization is regulated by anti-apoptotic BCL2-family proteins and by pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins such as BAX and BAK (Wei et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2001.

claim: Specific silencing of BAK significantly inhibits the apoptotic capacity of p40MET.
source: While specific silencing of BAK significantly inhibits the apoptotic capacity of p40MET, no evidence of direct interaction between p40MET and a BH3-only protein has been reported to date nor the mechanism involved (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: No evidence of direct interaction between p40MET and a BH3-only protein has been reported prior to this study.
source: While specific silencing of BAK significantly inhibits the apoptotic capacity of p40MET, no evidence of direct interaction between p40MET and a BH3-only protein has been reported to date nor the mechanism involved (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: Pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins have been described at the endoplasmic reticulum in addition to their outer mitochondrial membrane localization.
source: Besides their outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) localization, the pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins have also been described at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Zong et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zong et al., 2003.

claim: BH3-only proteins can interact with calcium channels such as IP3R at the ER.
source: In this organelle, they can interact with calcium channels such as inositol triphosphate receptors (IP3R) and thereby cause deregulation of the calcium flux between the ER and the mitochondria (Nutt et al., 2002; Scorrano et al., 2003; Zong et al., 2003; Oakes et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nutt et al., 2002; Scorrano et al., 2003; Zong et al., 2003; Oakes et al., 2005.

claim: BH3-only proteins can cause deregulation of calcium flux between the ER and mitochondria.
source: In this organelle, they can interact with calcium channels such as inositol triphosphate receptors (IP3R) and thereby cause deregulation of the calcium flux between the ER and the mitochondria (Nutt et al., 2002; Scorrano et al., 2003; Zong et al., 2003; Oakes et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nutt et al., 2002; Scorrano et al., 2003; Zong et al., 2003; Oakes et al., 2005.

claim: Calcium overload in the mitochondrial matrix causes membrane permeabilization through mPTP opening.
source: Several studies have shown calcium overload in the mitochondrial matrix to cause membrane permeabilization though mitochondrial Permeability Transition Pore (mPTP) opening that can trigger mitochondrial swelling and OMM disruption (for review see Brenner and Grimm, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Brenner and Grimm, 2006.

claim: mPTP opening can trigger mitochondrial swelling and outer mitochondrial membrane disruption.
source: Several studies have shown calcium overload in the mitochondrial matrix to cause membrane permeabilization though mitochondrial Permeability Transition Pore (mPTP) opening that can trigger mitochondrial swelling and OMM disruption (for review see Brenner and Grimm, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Brenner and Grimm, 2006.

claim: p40MET localizes to the mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) region.
source: In the present study, we have evidenced p40MET in the mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) region and have characterized p40MET-triggered calcium transfer from the ER to the mitochondria, which is important for its proapoptotic activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: p40MET triggers calcium transfer from the ER to the mitochondria.
source: In the present study, we have evidenced p40MET in the mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) region and have characterized p40MET-triggered calcium transfer from the ER to the mitochondria, which is important for its proapoptotic activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: p40MET-triggered calcium transfer from ER to mitochondria is important for its proapoptotic activity.
source: In the present study, we have evidenced p40MET in the mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) region and have characterized p40MET-triggered calcium transfer from the ER to the mitochondria, which is important for its proapoptotic activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Knock-in mice bearing a mutation of MET caspase cleavage site were generated.
source: We have also engineered a knock-in mouse model expressing MET mutated at caspase site in order to assess its importance in physiological apoptosis in vivo.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental model created.

claim: p40MET production is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis in vivo.
source: Knock-in mice bearing a mutation of MET caspase cleavage site highlighted that p40MET production is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis, and demonstrate that MET acts as a dependence receptor in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: MET acts as a dependence receptor in vivo.
source: Knock-in mice bearing a mutation of MET caspase cleavage site highlighted that p40MET production is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis, and demonstrate that MET acts as a dependence receptor in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: GFP-p40MET induces cytochrome C release in MCF10A epithelial cells.
source: In MCF10A epithelial cells, ectopic expression of GFP-p40MET induced cytochrome C release and caspase 3 cleavage as efficiently as the previously published flag-p40MET, in contrast to GFP-p40MET D1374N or GFP alone (Figure 1b–c; Figure 1—source data 1; and representative pictures in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c and supplementary figures.

claim: GFP-p40MET induces caspase 3 cleavage in MCF10A epithelial cells.
source: In MCF10A epithelial cells, ectopic expression of GFP-p40MET induced cytochrome C release and caspase 3 cleavage as efficiently as the previously published flag-p40MET, in contrast to GFP-p40MET D1374N or GFP alone (Figure 1b–c; Figure 1—source data 1; and representative pictures in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c and supplementary figures.

claim: GFP-p40MET D1374N does not induce cytochrome C release or caspase 3 cleavage in MCF10A cells.
source: In MCF10A epithelial cells, ectopic expression of GFP-p40MET induced cytochrome C release and caspase 3 cleavage as efficiently as the previously published flag-p40MET, in contrast to GFP-p40MET D1374N or GFP alone (Figure 1b–c; Figure 1—source data 1; and representative pictures in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c and supplementary figures.

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor treatment increases the proportion of p40MET-transfected cells displaying cytochrome-C release.
source: Furthermore, in p40MET-transfected cells, treatment with a pan-caspase inhibitor increased the proportion of cells displaying cytochrome-C release, a likely consequence of an inhibition of late apoptosis, which would impair apoptotic cell detachment and favor their detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor treatment impairs apoptotic cell detachment and favors detection of apoptotic cells.
source: Furthermore, in p40MET-transfected cells, treatment with a pan-caspase inhibitor increased the proportion of cells displaying cytochrome-C release, a likely consequence of an inhibition of late apoptosis, which would impair apoptotic cell detachment and favor their detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: BH3 mimetic treatment promotes p40MET generation in immortalized human hepatocytes (IHH).
source: In these cells, apoptosis induced by BH3 mimetic promoted p40MET generation, which was inhibited by pan-caspase inhibitor treatments and by MET silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor treatments inhibit p40MET generation in IHH cells.
source: In these cells, apoptosis induced by BH3 mimetic promoted p40MET generation, which was inhibited by pan-caspase inhibitor treatments and by MET silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MET silencing inhibits p40MET generation in IHH cells.
source: In these cells, apoptosis induced by BH3 mimetic promoted p40MET generation, which was inhibited by pan-caspase inhibitor treatments and by MET silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP-p40MET induces caspase 3 cleavage in IHH cells.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of GFP-p40MET in this cell line induced caspase 3 cleavage (Figure 1d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: p40MET co-localizes with FACL4, a protein residing mostly in MAMs.
source: We thus examined whether p40MET might co-localize with Fatty Acid CoA Ligase 4 (FACL4), a protein residing mostly in MAMs, and this proved to be the case (Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: p40MET D1374N fragment co-localizes with FACL4.
source: FACL4 was also found to colocalize with the p40MET D1374N fragment, but not with GFP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: GFP does not co-localize with FACL4.
source: FACL4 was also found to colocalize with the p40MET D1374N fragment, but not with GFP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: Endogenous p40MET is found exclusively in the MAM fraction after subcellular fractionation.
source: p40MET was found exclusively in the MAM fraction, in agreement with the immunofluorescence.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations from subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 1f.

claim: BAK siRNA abrogates MET fragment induced caspase 3 activation in MCF10A cells.
source: In MCF10A, BAK siRNA abrogated MET fragment induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release, BOK silencing partially inhibited them, while BAX silencing had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: BAK siRNA abrogates MET fragment induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: In MCF10A, BAK siRNA abrogated MET fragment induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release, BOK silencing partially inhibited them, while BAX silencing had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: BOK silencing partially inhibits p40MET-induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: In MCF10A, BAK siRNA abrogated MET fragment induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release, BOK silencing partially inhibited them, while BAX silencing had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: BAX silencing has no effect on p40MET-induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: In MCF10A, BAK siRNA abrogated MET fragment induced caspase 3 activation and cytochrome C release, BOK silencing partially inhibited them, while BAX silencing had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: BAK is mainly involved in p40MET-induced apoptosis.
source: These results are consistent with our previous study on the impact of BAK and BAX silencing on the apoptosis of MCF10A cells transfected with p40MET-Flag (Lefebvre et al., 2013) and confirmed the main involvement of BAK in p40MET-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and supported by citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: Co-transfection of BAK-mT2 and BCL-XL-SYFP2 leads to a mean FRET efficiency of 8%.
source: As a positive control, BAK-mT2 and BCL-XL-SYFP2 co-transfection led to a mean FRET efficiency of 8% (in agreement with what can be obtained for other heteromeric proteins), while it was negligible (<0.1%) with vector encoding freely diffusing SYFP2 (Figure 2b; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Co-transfection of BAK-mT2 and freely diffusing SYFP2 leads to negligible FRET efficiency (<0.1%).
source: As a positive control, BAK-mT2 and BCL-XL-SYFP2 co-transfection led to a mean FRET efficiency of 8% (in agreement with what can be obtained for other heteromeric proteins), while it was negligible (<0.1%) with vector encoding freely diffusing SYFP2 (Figure 2b; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Co-transfection of BAK-mT2 and p40MET-SYFP2 gives rise to FRET efficiency of about 2.5%.
source: Co-transfection with the vectors encoding BAK-mT2 and p40MET-SYFP2also gave rise to FRET about 2.5% efficiency (Figure 2b; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Co-transfection of p40MET-mT2 and BAK-SYFP2 gives rise to a mean FRET efficiency of 4%.
source: In the reverse donor-acceptor configuration, we found a mean FRET efficiency of 4% confirming the interaction (Figure 2c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: p40MET interacts with BAK as demonstrated by FRET experiments.
source: In the reverse donor-acceptor configuration, we found a mean FRET efficiency of 4% confirming the interaction (Figure 2c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: FRET occurs between p40MET and BAX with mean values of 2.5% and 4.3%.
source: We also noticed a FRET phenomenon occurring between p40MET and BAX (with mean values respectively at 2.5% and 4.3%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–b; Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–b.

claim: p40MET-mT2 hardly interacts with BCL-XL (1.5% mean FRET efficiency).
source: In contrast, p40MET-mT2 hardly interacted with BCL-XL (1.5% mean FRET efficiency).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: The study of p40MET interaction with BOK resulted in negative output.
source: In a similar way, the study of p40MET interaction with BOK resulted in negative output (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1) whereas a strong interaction between BOK and BCL-XL was evidenced.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–c.

claim: A strong interaction between BOK and BCL-XL was evidenced.
source: In a similar way, the study of p40MET interaction with BOK resulted in negative output (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1) whereas a strong interaction between BOK and BCL-XL was evidenced.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: FRET efficiency of 1.5% was found for transfer from mT2-p40MET to SYFP2-BAK in IHH cells.
source: We actually found a 1.5% FRET efficiency (p<0.05) for a transfer from mT2-p40MET to SYFP2-BAK and 5.0% for a transfer from mT2-BAK to SYFP2-p40MET (p<0.001) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d–e; Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d–e.

claim: FRET efficiency of 5.0% was found for transfer from mT2-BAK to SYFP2-p40MET in IHH cells.
source: We actually found a 1.5% FRET efficiency (p<0.05) for a transfer from mT2-p40MET to SYFP2-BAK and 5.0% for a transfer from mT2-BAK to SYFP2-p40MET (p<0.001) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d–e; Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d–e.

claim: The interaction between p40MET and BAK is confirmed in liver-derived cell lines.
source: The interaction between p40MET and BAK is thus confirmed in these liver-derived cell lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data in IHH cells.

claim: No FRET was detected between BAK-mT2 and IP3R1-EYFP.
source: No FRET was detected between BAK-mT2 or p40MET-mT2 and IP3R1-EYFP (Figure 2b–c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b–c.

claim: No FRET was detected between p40MET-mT2 and IP3R1-EYFP.
source: No FRET was detected between BAK-mT2 or p40MET-mT2 and IP3R1-EYFP (Figure 2b–c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b–c.

claim: p40MET contains a putative BH3 domain with an LXXXXD core motif conserved in mice and humans.
source: Alignment of BH3 domain from BH3-only and BH3-like proteins with p40MET sequence revealed a putative BH3 domain with an LXXXXD core motif conserved in mice and humans (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a.

claim: Mutation of L1110 and D1115 residues in GFP-p40MET abrogates its pro-apoptotic activity.
source: Mutation of the corresponding L1110 and D1115 residues in GFP-p40MET abrogated its pro-apoptotic activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 5b–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5b–c.

claim: Mutation of the potential BH3-like domain of p40MET decreases its interaction with BAK.
source: Furthermore, FRET experiments with plasmids encoding mT2-p40MET and SYFP2-p40MET mutated or not on L and D residues (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–b) showed that mutation of the potential BH3-like domain of p40MET decreased its interaction with BAK (Figure 2d–e; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d–e.

claim: p40MET interacts directly with BAK through a putative BH3-like domain.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that p40MET interacts directly with BAK through a putative BH3-like domain and that this partner might participate in the pro-apoptotic action of p40MET.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: BAK participates in the pro-apoptotic action of p40MET.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that p40MET interacts directly with BAK through a putative BH3-like domain and that this partner might participate in the pro-apoptotic action of p40MET.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: p40MET-induced cytochrome C release is inhibited in MCF10A cells cultured in Ca2+-free medium.
source: We found p40MET-induced cytochrome C release to be inhibited in MCF10A cells cultured in Ca2+-free medium (Figure 3a; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ca2+ chelation prevents p40MET-induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: In addition, Ca2+ chelation prevented p40MET-induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells or caspase 3 activation in IHH (Figure 3b–c; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b–c.

claim: Ca2+ chelation prevents p40MET-induced caspase 3 activation in IHH cells.
source: In addition, Ca2+ chelation prevented p40MET-induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells or caspase 3 activation in IHH (Figure 3b–c; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b–c.

claim: Treatment with xestospongin B, an IP3R inhibitor, inhibits p40MET-induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: Similar inhibition of cytochrome C release in MCF10A were observed upon treatment with xestospongin B, a potent IP3R inhibitor (Figure 3d; Figure 3—source data 1), or with an siRNA against MCU (Figure 3e–f; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: siRNA against MCU inhibits p40MET-induced cytochrome C release in MCF10A cells.
source: Similar inhibition of cytochrome C release in MCF10A were observed upon treatment with xestospongin B, a potent IP3R inhibitor (Figure 3d; Figure 3—source data 1), or with an siRNA against MCU (Figure 3e–f; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e–f.

claim: Apoptosis induced by staurosporine is unaffected by calcium-related treatments.
source: Apoptosis induced by staurosporine was unaffected by such treatments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: A Ca2+ flux between the ER and mitochondria is required for p40MET-induced cytochrome C release from the mitochondria.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that a Ca2+ flux between the ER and mitochondria is required for p40MET-induced cytochrome C release from the mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: GFP-p40MET-expressing cells show a significantly lower Fura-2 fluorescence peak than cells expressing GFP-p40MET D1374N or GFP after thapsigargin addition.
source: After thapsigargin addition, GFP-p40MET-expressing cells showed a significantly lower Fura-2 fluorescence peak than cells expressing GFP-p40MET D1374N or GFP (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The ER Ca2+ pool is depleted after p40MET transfection.
source: This suggests that the ER Ca2+ pool was depleted after p40MET transfection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fura-2 fluorescence data.

claim: p40MET transfection increases FRET efficiency by 26% in cells with 4mtD3cpv biosensor.
source: We found p40MET transfection to increase the FRET efficiency by 26% (p=0.0013) as compared to transfection with a control plasmid, suggesting a substantial increase of the calcium concentration in mitochondria (Figure 3h; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: p40MET transfection causes a substantial increase of calcium concentration in mitochondria.
source: We found p40MET transfection to increase the FRET efficiency by 26% (p=0.0013) as compared to transfection with a control plasmid, suggesting a substantial increase of the calcium concentration in mitochondria (Figure 3h; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET efficiency data.

claim: mPTP inhibition by cyclosporin A reduces p40MET-induced apoptosis.
source: As suspected, mPTP inhibition by cyclosporin A was found to reduce the p40MET-induced apoptosis (Figure 3i; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: p40MET impairs ER-to-mitochondria calcium homeostasis, causing mitochondrial calcium overload and permeabilization.
source: Altogether, these data show that p40MET impairs the ER-to-mitochondria calcium homeostasis, eventually causing a mitochondrial calcium overload and permeabilization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: A knock-in mouse model was developed where the Met gene locus is modified at the C-terminal caspase site with D1374N mutation.
source: To investigate the in vivo involvement of MET cleavage in apoptosis, we used Cre-Lox recombination to develop a knock-in mouse model where the Met gene locus is modified in the C-terminal caspase site (Figure 4a–b). The mutation introduced is D1374N, as in the above-described in vitro experiments, and it prevents C-terminal cleavage.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the mouse model and Figure 4a–b.

claim: The D1374N mutation prevents C-terminal cleavage of MET.
source: The mutation introduced is D1374N, as in the above-described in vitro experiments, and it prevents C-terminal cleavage.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of the mutation.

claim: D1374N Mouse Embryonic Fibroblasts (MEFs) are more resistant than wild-type to anisomycin treatment.
source: First results showing D1374N Mouse Embryonic Fibroblasts (MEFs) to be more resistant than wild-type to anisomycin treatment evidenced the importance of the caspase cleavage site for optimal apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: The caspase cleavage site is important for optimal apoptosis.
source: First results showing D1374N Mouse Embryonic Fibroblasts (MEFs) to be more resistant than wild-type to anisomycin treatment evidenced the importance of the caspase cleavage site for optimal apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations in MEFs.

claim: WT and D1374N BMEL clones display comparable BMEL marker expression.
source: We selected two WT clones (A and B) and two D1374N clones (A and B) displaying comparable BMEL marker expression quantified by RT-Q-PCR (Krt19, Hnf4a as BMEL markers; Aldob, Alb, as markers of differentiated hepatocytes) (Figure 4c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: WT and D1374N BMEL clones show comparable doubling times.
source: We first found WT and D1374N BMEL clones to show comparable doubling times (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: HGF/SF stimulation induces islet scattering with equal efficiency in WT and D1374N BMEL clones.
source: In addition, HGF/SF stimulation induced islet scattering with equal efficiency in the WT and D1374N clones (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The D1374N MET mutation does not alter HGF-induced MET phosphorylation.
source: The D1374N MET mutation likewise did not alter either HGF-induced MET phosphorylation or AKT and ERK phosphorylation (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The D1374N MET mutation does not alter HGF-induced AKT and ERK phosphorylation.
source: The D1374N MET mutation likewise did not alter either HGF-induced MET phosphorylation or AKT and ERK phosphorylation (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Staurosporine treatment leads to generation of p40MET fragment in WT BMEL cells.
source: Lastly, massive apoptosis induced by a 7 hr staurosporine treatment led to generation of the p40MET fragment in the WT cells and of a slightly longer p40MET D1374N fragment in the D1374N cells, in agreement with the presence of the C-terminal tail, which was prevented by pan-caspase inhibitors (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Staurosporine treatment leads to generation of a slightly longer p40MET D1374N fragment in D1374N BMEL cells.
source: Lastly, massive apoptosis induced by a 7 hr staurosporine treatment led to generation of the p40MET fragment in the WT cells and of a slightly longer p40MET D1374N fragment in the D1374N cells, in agreement with the presence of the C-terminal tail, which was prevented by pan-caspase inhibitors (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitors prevent generation of p40MET fragments in BMEL cells.
source: Lastly, massive apoptosis induced by a 7 hr staurosporine treatment led to generation of the p40MET fragment in the WT cells and of a slightly longer p40MET D1374N fragment in the D1374N cells, in agreement with the presence of the C-terminal tail, which was prevented by pan-caspase inhibitors (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: MET D1374N BMEL cells form small clusters when cultured without collagen coating, while WT cells fail to grow.
source: Whereas the WT cells failed to grow under these conditions, MET D1374N BMEL cells formed small clusters from day 2, showing a better capacity to cope with the loss of matrix-driven signals (Figure 5a; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MET D1374N BMEL cells show better capacity to cope with loss of matrix-driven signals than WT cells.
source: Whereas the WT cells failed to grow under these conditions, MET D1374N BMEL cells formed small clusters from day 2, showing a better capacity to cope with the loss of matrix-driven signals (Figure 5a; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Staurosporine treatment induces caspase 3 and PARP cleavages in WT BMEL cells but not in MET D1374N cells.
source: While staurosporine treatment induced caspase 3 and PARP cleavages in the WT cells, these cleavages were undetected in the MET D1374N cells (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: MET D1374N BMEL cells are more resistant than WT cells to staurosporine-induced apoptosis.
source: Immunostaining for cleaved caspase 3 further showed the MET D1374N cells to be more resistant than the WT cells to staurosporine-induced apoptosis (Figure 5c; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Resistance to apoptosis in MET D1374N cells was also observed upon BH3 mimetic ABT737 treatment.
source: Resistance to apoptosis in MET D1374N cells was also observed upon BH3 mimetic ABT737 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MET cleavage is important for apoptosis amplification in hepatic progenitors.
source: These results demonstrate the importance of MET cleavage for apoptosis amplification in hepatic progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in BMEL cells.

claim: A lower percentage of MET D1374N BMEL cells than WT cells display staurosporine-induced caspase activation.
source: First, a lower percentage of MET D1374N BMEL cells than WT cells displayed staurosporine-induced caspase activation as shown above (Figure 5d; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Only WT BMEL cells respond to IP3R inhibitor xestospongin in terms of caspase activation.
source: Second, only the WT population responded to the additional presence of the IP3R inhibitor xestospongin, confirming involvement of Ca2+ flux for p40MET induced cell death.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: Ca2+ flux is involved in p40MET induced cell death.
source: Second, only the WT population responded to the additional presence of the IP3R inhibitor xestospongin, confirming involvement of Ca2+ flux for p40MET induced cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the xestospongin experiment.

claim: After staurosporine treatment, MET D1374N BMEL cells take up Ca2+ more efficiently than WT cells initially.
source: After the first injections, MET D1374N cells took up Ca2+ more efficiently than WT cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations from calcium uptake assays.

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake stops at a total concentration of 100 µM in WT BMEL cells versus 140 µM for MET D1374N cells.
source: Furthermore, on average, mitochondrial uptake stopped in the WT cells at a total concentration of 100 µM, versus 140 µM for the MET D1374N cells (Figure 5e–f; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e–f.

claim: Staurosporine-treated WT BMEL cells have lower Ca2+ uptake capacity than MET D1374N BMEL cells, suggesting WT cells are already overloaded with Ca2+.
source: This lower Ca2+ uptake capacity of staurosporine-treated WT BMEL cells as compared to MET D1374N BMEL cells suggests that the former are already overloaded with Ca2+, possibly because of p40MET generation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium uptake data.

claim: WT and MET D1374N mice display no obvious phenotypic differences.
source: WT and MET D1374N mice displayed no obvious phenotypic differences and interbreeding between WT, D1374N, and heterozygous mice gave the expected Mendelian distributions (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6a–b.

claim: Interbreeding between WT, D1374N, and heterozygous mice gives expected Mendelian distributions.
source: WT and MET D1374N mice displayed no obvious phenotypic differences and interbreeding between WT, D1374N, and heterozygous mice gave the expected Mendelian distributions (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: D1374N mice do not display notable developmental anomalies.
source: D1374N mice did not display any notable developmental anomalies in agreement with a functional pro-survival MET signaling.
evidence: This is a direct statement about observations in the mouse model.

claim: D1374N mice have normal liver and mammary gland organization.
source: We also looked more carefully at the organization of the liver and mammary glands, organs known to require MET activity for their proper morphogenesis, which displayed normal organization (Figure 6c; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HGF/SF production promotes hepatocyte survival in FAS-induced fulminant hepatitis.
source: To investigate the sensitivity of WT and MET D3174N mouse liver tissues to apoptosis, we focused on FAS-induced fulminant hepatitis, a condition in which HGF/SF production is reported to promote hepatocyte survival (Kosai et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kosai et al., 1998.

claim: HGF/SF induces a survival response in primary hepatic progenitors that is reduced by crizotinib.
source: HGF/SF was indeed able to induce a survival response in primary hepatic progenitors and this response was reduced by crizotinib (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–b.

claim: Four hours after FAS injection, WT mice display more caspase 3 activation than D1374N mice.
source: Four hours after FAS injection, the WT mice displayed more caspase 3 activation than D1374N mice, with respectively 62% (8/13) and 27% (2/15) highly positive livers.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: 62% of WT mice have highly positive livers for caspase 3 activation after FAS injection versus 27% of D1374N mice.
source: Four hours after FAS injection, the WT mice displayed more caspase 3 activation than D1374N mice, with respectively 62% (8/13) and 27% (2/15) highly positive livers.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: Only 8% of WT livers were negative for caspase 3 activation after FAS injection, as opposed to 47% of D1374N livers.
source: Conversely, only one WT liver out of 13 (8%) was found negative for caspase 3 activation, as opposed to 47% (7/15) of the D1374N livers (Figure 6e; Figure 6—source data 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 3b for a complete-panel illustration), clearly demonstrating the resistance of MET D1374N mice to apoptosis induction, with respect to WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 3b.

claim: MET D1374N mice are resistant to apoptosis induction compared to WT mice.
source: Conversely, only one WT liver out of 13 (8%) was found negative for caspase 3 activation, as opposed to 47% (7/15) of the D1374N livers (Figure 6e; Figure 6—source data 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 3b for a complete-panel illustration), clearly demonstrating the resistance of MET D1374N mice to apoptosis induction, with respect to WT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the caspase 3 activation data.

claim: 92% of WT mice were positive for cleaved caspase 3 staining after FAS injection, compared to 53% of MET D1374N mice.
source: Overall, 92% (12/13) of the WT mice were positive for cleaved caspase 3 staining, as compared to 53% (8/15) of the MET D1374N mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: 82% of WT mice doubled their plasma ALAT levels after FAS injection versus 46% of MET D1374N mice.
source: Four hours after FAS injection, 82% of WT mice (14/17) had doubled their plasma ALAT levels vs only 46% (5/13) of MET D1374N mice (Figure 6f; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: All WT mice doubled their plasma ASAT levels after FAS injection versus 70% of MET D1374N mice.
source: Similarly, the plasma ASAT levels had doubled for all WT mice (17/17) vs 70% of MET D1374N (9/13) mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: MET D1374N mice display resistance to FAS-induced apoptosis.
source: The MET D1374N mice thus displayed resistance to FAS-induced apoptosis, which demonstrates the importance of MET C-terminal caspase cleavage for optimal apoptosis in vivo and highlights MET function as a dependence receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: MET C-terminal caspase cleavage is important for optimal apoptosis in vivo.
source: The MET D1374N mice thus displayed resistance to FAS-induced apoptosis, which demonstrates the importance of MET C-terminal caspase cleavage for optimal apoptosis in vivo and highlights MET function as a dependence receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in the mouse model.

claim: MAMs constitute a subdomain with direct interactions between the ER and mitochondria.
source: MAMs constitute a subdomain with direct interactions between the ER and mitochondria.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about MAMs.

claim: MAMs play a crucial role in amplifying cell death.
source: They notably play a crucial role in amplifying cell death (Naon and Scorrano, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Naon and Scorrano, 2014.

claim: BCL2 proteins localize to both the ER and mitochondria, both localizations being involved in apoptosis regulation.
source: Indeed, beside their localization at the outer membrane of mitochondria, BCL2 proteins were found localized at the ER, both localization being involved in apoptosis regulation (Scorrano et al., 2003; Rong et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scorrano et al., 2003 and Rong et al., 2008.

claim: BAK has been described to play a role in promoting Ca2+ release from the ER.
source: Because, BAK has been described to play a role in this process by promoting Ca2+ release from the ER (Scorrano et al., 2003), we checked for a possible involvement of Ca2+ in p40MET-induced apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scorrano et al., 2003.

claim: Bcl-2 and Bcl-XL can interact with IP3R channels and modulate ER Ca2+ homeostasis, promoting apoptosis resistance.
source: The anti-apoptotic members Bcl-2 and Bcl-XL can interact with IP3R channels and modulate ER Ca2+ homeostasis, thus promoting apoptosis resistance (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: BAX and BAK can induce massive calcium leakage from the ER, followed by mitochondrial Ca2+ accumulation and apoptosis.
source: Conversely, the pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and BAK can induce massive calcium leakage from the ER, followed by mitochondrial Ca2+ accumulation and apoptosis (Nutt et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nutt et al., 2002.

claim: BAK facilitates calcium transfer by promoting contacts between mitochondria and the ER.
source: Recent findings demonstrate that BAK facilitates calcium transfer by promoting contacts between mitochondria and the ER (Mebratu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mebratu et al., 2017.

claim: BAK silencing reduces p40MET-induced apoptosis.
source: We have previously reported BAK silencing or Bcl-XL overexpression to reduce p40MET-induced apoptosis (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: Bcl-XL overexpression reduces p40MET-induced apoptosis.
source: We have previously reported BAK silencing or Bcl-XL overexpression to reduce p40MET-induced apoptosis (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2013.

claim: p40MET interacts with BAK but not Bcl-XL as shown by FRET experiments.
source: Interestingly, the results of our FRET experiments show that p40MET interacts with BAK but not Bcl-XL.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FRET experimental data.

claim: Upon MET cleavage by caspases, p40MET is released into the cytoplasm where it interacts with BAK at MAMs.
source: In the light of our various findings, we propose that upon MET cleavage by caspases, p40MET is released into the cytoplasm where it interacts with BAK at MAMs and promotes a Ca2+ flux from the ER to the mitochondria, causing mitochondrial permeabilization and apoptosis amplification (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: p40MET promotes Ca2+ flux from the ER to the mitochondria, causing mitochondrial permeabilization and apoptosis amplification.
source: In the light of our various findings, we propose that upon MET cleavage by caspases, p40MET is released into the cytoplasm where it interacts with BAK at MAMs and promotes a Ca2+ flux from the ER to the mitochondria, causing mitochondrial permeabilization and apoptosis amplification (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Dependence receptors display a great variety of mechanisms to promote apoptosis.
source: Dependence receptors displayed a great variety of mechanisms to promote apoptosis (Negulescu and Mehlen, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Negulescu and Mehlen, 2018.

claim: DCC and UNC5H receptors undergo caspase cleavage and act as caspase activators through death-domain unmasked by cleavage.
source: For example, both DCC and UNC5H receptors undergo caspase cleavage and act as caspase activators though death-domain unmasked by the cleavage and carried by the part that remains membrane-anchored (Mehlen et al., 1998; Llambi et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehlen et al., 1998 and Llambi et al., 2001.

claim: TrkC receptor releases a pro-apoptotic fragment upon caspase cleavage which shuttles to mitochondria and promotes BAX activation.
source: The TrkC receptor, on the other hand, releases upon caspase cleavage a pro-apoptotic fragment which shuttles to the mitochondria and promotes BAX activation (Ichim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ichim et al., 2013.

claim: This is the first time a dependence receptor has been shown to act via regulation of Ca2+ flux.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a dependence receptor has been shown to act via regulation of the Ca2+ flux.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Knock-out of the Met or Hgf/sf gene is lethal in utero and leads to reduced liver size associated with decreased hepatocyte proliferation.
source: Knock-out of the Met or Hgf/sf gene is lethal in utero and leads to a reduced liver size associated with decreased hepatocyte proliferation (Schmidt et al., 1995; Uehara et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 1995 and Uehara et al., 1995.

claim: Altered liver regeneration has been found in MET-deficient mice.
source: Furthermore, altered liver regeneration has been found in MET-deficient mice (Huh et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huh et al., 2004.

claim: Liver and mammary gland organogenesis are not affected by the MET D1374N mutation.
source: We have found that liver and mammary gland organogenesis, both of which depend on MET pro-survival signaling, are not affected by the MET D1374N mutation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about findings in the mouse model.

claim: Overexpression of the ligand of the DCC dependence receptor inhibits its pro-apoptotic activity and can promote spontaneous adenoma formation.
source: Overexpression of the ligand of the Deleted in Colorectal Cancer (DCC) dependence receptor inhibits its pro-apoptotic activity and can promote spontaneous adenoma formation (Mazelin et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mazelin et al., 2004.

claim: DCC acts as a conditional tumor suppressor gene.
source: Although DCC-deficient mice (like MET D1374N mice, data not shown) do not develop spontaneous tumors, experiments in which they were crossed with mice bearing a cancer-predisposing APC mutation suggest that DCC acts as a conditional tumor suppressor gene (Castets et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Castets et al., 2012.

claim: The COSMIC database lists six MET mutations affecting the MET caspase sites in various cancers.
source: In agreement with this concept, the COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer) database lists six MET mutations affecting the MET caspase sites in various cancers.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data from the COSMIC database.

claim: Exon 14 splice-site mutations are found in 3% of pulmonary tumors and lead to loss of the MET juxtamembrane domain.
source: Also described are exon 14 splice-site mutations found in 3% of pulmonary tumors and leading to loss of the MET juxtamembrane domain, which contains the caspase site leading to p40MET release (Duplaquet et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duplaquet et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple MET-caspase-cleavage-abolishing mutations support the notion that MET pro-apoptotic function might put a brake on tumorigenesis.
source: Altogether, the presence of these multiple MET-caspase-cleavage-abolishing mutations supports the notion that the MET pro-apoptotic function might put a brake on tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutation data.
